title: Lab 8
text:
In this lab, we will explore and visualize the data using the tidyverse suite of packages, and perform statistical inference using infer. The data we are using will be coming from openintro.
Let’s load the packages.

library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(infer)




You will be analyzing the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS) survey, which uses data from high schoolers to help discover health patterns. The dataset is called yrbss.






Exercise 1



What are the counts within each category for the amount of days these students have texted while driving within the past 30 days?








Exercise 2



What is the proportion of people who have texted while driving every day in the past 30 days and never wear helmets?


Remember that you can use filter to limit the dataset to just non-helmet wearers. Here, we will name the dataset no_helmet.

no_helmet <- yrbss |>
  filter(helmet_12m == "never")

Also, it may be easier to calculate the proportion if you create a new variable that specifies whether the individual has texted every day while driving over the past 30 days or not. We will call this variable text_ind.

no_helmet <- no_helmet |>
  mutate(text_ind = factor(ifelse(text_while_driving_30d == "30", "yes", "no")))

Remember that you can use filter to limit the dataset to just non-helmet wearers. Here, we will name the dataset no_helmet.

title: Lab 8
text:
Inference on proportions
When summarizing the YRBSS, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention seeks insight into the population parameters. To do this, you can answer the question, “What proportion of people in your sample reported that they have texted while driving each day for the past 30 days?” with a statistic; while the question “What proportion of people on earth have texted while driving each day for the past 30 days?” is answered with an estimate of the parameter.
The inferential tools for estimating population proportion are analogous to those used for means in the last chapter: the confidence interval and the hypothesis test.

no_helmet <- na.omit(no_helmet)

no_helmet |>
  specify(response = text_ind, success = "yes") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "prop") |>
  get_ci(level = 0.95)

Note that since the goal is to construct an interval estimate for a proportion, it’s necessary to both include the success argument within specify, which accounts for the proportion of non-helmet wearers than have consistently texted while driving the past 30 days, in this example, and that stat within calculate is here “prop”, signaling that you are trying to do some sort of inference on a proportion.






Exercise 3



What is the margin of error for the estimate of the proportion of non-helmet wearers that have texted while driving each day for the past 30 days based on this survey?








Exercise 4



Using the infer package, calculate confidence intervals for two other categorical variables (you’ll need to decide which level to call “success”, and report the associated margins of error. Interpret the interval in context of the data. It may be helpful to create new data sets for each of the two countries first, and then use these data sets to construct the confidence intervals.

title: Lab 8
text:
Hypothesis testing
One function to recall that will be helpful to quickly calculate proportions with categorical data is the table() function. This will tell you the number of individuals in each category, allowing you to calculate proportions.
For example, if we wanted to calculate the proportion of individuals who texted while driving in the last 30 days:

table(no_helmet$text_ind)

If we didn’t want to do the math, we can use prop.table() as a wrapper for table():

prop.table(table(no_helmet$text_ind))


One proportion test
We can use the prop.test() function in order to perform a one-proportion test. It is best used when your sample size is greater than 30; we’re safe with this data! It takes the arguments prop.test(x, n, p, alternative = "two.sided", correct = TRUE), where x = # of successes, n = total sample size, p = null probability, alternative = type of null hypotheses (defaults to ‘not equal’; can also use “greater” and “less”), and correct = whether or not to use Yates’ continuity correction. NOTE: you will generally set correct = FALSE rather than the default of TRUE.


Two proportion test
A two proportion test uses the same function with the same arguments provided as the one proportion test. However, there are two changes. First, for x: rather than provide a single number, we need to provide it a vector. This will look like x = c(success1, success2). And, the second change is with n: it also gets a vector. This looks like n = c(count1, count2). With these, success1 is the number of success in group1, which is of size count1. Same for success2 and count2 - they belong to your second group.
For example, we could see if the proportion of folks who wore helmets and texted was different than those who did not.
We first need to make our data:

full_data <- yrbss

full_data <- full_data |>
  mutate(helmet_ind = ifelse(helmet_12m == "never", "no", 
                             ifelse(helmet_12m == "did not ride", NA, "yes")))

full_data <- full_data |>
  mutate(text_ind = ifelse(text_while_driving_30d == "30", "yes", "no"))

Then, we might think our next step would be to see what our proportions are for each group. Note how we are telling R we want a table made of two different columns. It is important to remember that your first argument (helmet_ind here) will be your rows, and the second will be the columns.

prop.table(table(full_data$helmet_ind, full_data$text_ind))

Notice anything strange about the numbers?






Exercise 5



When using prop.table() for two variables, how does R calculate the proportions? It may be useful to do the math yourself using a table().


We will use the numbers obtained from table() for our prop.test() function:

prop.test(x = c(56, 463), n = c(1656, 6503), correct = FALSE)

We see from the results that the groups are indeed different (p < 0.001!), and folks who do not wear a helmet are more likely to text and drive than those who do not.






Exercise 6



Using the data available, write a one-proportion and a two-proportion research question and run a hypothesis test on them. Be sure to write your conclusion in terms of your question! (i.e., you will have a total of two research questions, two inferential tests, and two conclusions)
